projects.title: Lowering the Threshold to Psychological Care
projects.heroAlt: Calm onboarding screen for a digital mental health service with symptom-first copy and low-intensity imagery
projects.alt: Prototype of a symptom-first onboarding flow for a mental health service
projects.description: Self-initiated conceptual redesign of Din Psykolog’s onboarding experience, exploring how decision sequencing shapes perceived safety in vulnerable moments. Through experience-based language, guided matching, and delayed commitment signals, the concept lowers early friction while preserving security and clinical integrity.
projects.metaDescription: A self-initiated redesign of Din Psykolog's onboarding that lowers the threshold to psychological care through guided matching and delayed commitment.
projects.fullDescription:
This is a self-initiated conceptual redesign exploring alternative structural decisions within an existing digital mental health service.

Rather than focusing on interface polish, the project examines how decision sequencing, language, and commitment timing influence perceived safety and responsibility in vulnerable contexts.
projects.problem:
In the onboarding journey I analyzed, users were asked to choose a psychologist, select a time, and authenticate early in the process.

Clinical terminology and early commitment signals introduced evaluation and responsibility before sufficient clarity had been established.

This sequencing may increase perceived decision pressure in an already vulnerable context.

insight.text:
Digital care reduces structural barriers to access. Yet even when services are available, the psychological cost of initiating care can remain high.

In moments of emotional uncertainty, users are not only evaluating options — they are evaluating themselves. When high-commitment actions precede need clarification, responsibility shifts toward the user at a moment of uncertainty. This can contribute to decision anxiety and early drop-off.

In the version analyzed, strong authentication was introduced before users had clarified their needs, signaling commitment during exploration.

By introducing guidance before choice — and postponing authentication until booking becomes imminent — the system absorbs uncertainty instead of amplifying it.
insight.alt: Visualization of the original onboarding flow highlighting early evaluation and authentication points

projects.approach:
The onboarding was redesigned around three structural principles: recognition before choice, guidance before evaluation, and delayed commitment.

The flow begins with experience recognition rather than diagnostic labels, reducing pressure to self-define prematurely.

Users then choose how they prefer to be matched: through system-assisted recommendations or direct browsing. This preserves autonomy while reducing early comparison pressure.

Optional refinements are placed within progressive disclosure components, clearly signaling that they are supportive rather than required.

Strong authentication is introduced only when booking becomes imminent, separating identity verification from exploration.
projects.outcome:
The redesigned flow reduces perceived entry barriers, creates clearer continuity between steps, and shifts responsibility from user to system.

Authentication is reframed as protection rather than obligation, and symptom selection supports recognition instead of self-diagnosis.

Together, these structural adjustments are intended to reduce early friction while maintaining clinical integrity and security standards.
projects.prototypeBody:
The flow consists of progressive stages: experience recognition, matching preference selection, system-assisted recommendation, optional refinement, booking, and identity verification prior to confirmation.

Each stage introduces higher-commitment actions only after clarity has increased.

Microcopy normalizes uncertainty, choices are reversible, and visual intensity is intentionally restrained to reduce overwhelm.
projects.disclaimer: This is a self-initiated conceptual redesign and is not affiliated with or endorsed by Din Psykolog. The project is intended for exploratory and educational purposes only.
projects.reflection:
This project reinforced that friction is not neutral in vulnerable contexts.

The order of decisions directly influences whether users feel supported or overwhelmed. Designing for mental health requires intentional sequencing, restrained language, and clear boundaries between exploration and commitment.

Small structural adjustments can significantly shift how safe and capable users feel at the moment of starting.

images.title: Guidance Before Choice

projects.title: Swipe-based App Review Tool
projects.heroAlt: Mobile prototype showing swipe-based review interface with product card and gesture indicators
projects.alt: Prototype of a swipe-based app review flow
projects.description: A low-friction review flow designed to help users give quick, intuitive feedback through swipe interactions. The concept explores how gesture-based input can reduce review fatigue while maintaining clarity and engagement.
projects.metaDescription: A swipe-based review flow that cut review completion time by 40% in user testing, making app feedback quick and intuitive.
projects.fullDescription: A low-friction review flow designed to help users give quick, intuitive feedback through swipe interactions. The concept explores how gesture-based input can reduce review fatigue while maintaining clarity and engagement.
projects.problem: Traditional review forms require too much effort for low-stakes feedback, leading to user abandonment. The challenge was to create a gesture-based review system that feels natural and intuitive while maintaining clarity about what users are giving feedback on.
projects.approach: I designed a swipe-based card interface where each card represents a single product or review prompt. Users can swipe left/right to give feedback quickly. I used Figma for rapid prototyping and tested the interaction model to ensure reliable gesture recognition and feedback clarity.
projects.outcome: The prototype successfully demonstrated a 40% reduction in review completion time compared to traditional forms. The swipe interaction proved intuitive for users without training, and the card-based layout maintained context awareness throughout the review flow.
projects.prototypeBody: The swipe interaction was prototyped using Smart Animate and directional drag zones. Due to limitations in Figma’s gesture handling, such as the lack of directional thresholds and state-scoped navigation, navigation was triggered as part of the drag interaction rather than after animation completion. This approach ensured reliable feedback and a consistent experience during testing.
projects.reflection: This project taught me how powerful gesture-based interactions can be when designed thoughtfully. The key takeaway was that reducing friction doesn't mean reducing clarity—both can be achieved simultaneously through careful iteration and user testing.

images.title: Card-Based Review Flow
images.description: Each card presents a single review prompt, allowing users to focus on one decision at a time. By limiting visible choices, the interface reduces cognitive load and makes it easier to give quick, confident feedback through swipe gestures.
images.alt: Mobile interface showing a card-based review flow with swipe gestures

images.title: Measurable Improvements
images.description: User testing demonstrated a 40% reduction in review completion time compared to traditional forms. The gesture-based approach proved intuitive even for first-time users, eliminating the need for onboarding tutorials.

projects.title: Exploitation by Design
projects.heroAlt: Research visualization showing categorized dark patterns identified in social media interfaces
projects.alt: Research-based case study on dark patterns in social media interfaces
projects.description: A research-driven UX case study investigating how dark patterns in social media mobile applications manipulate user behavior and undermine user autonomy. Download the full thesis in Swedish.
projects.metaDescription: A UX research study of nine social media apps that identified 34 dark patterns, 13 newly defined, and how they undermine user autonomy.
projects.fullDescription: An in-depth UX research project examining the prevalence of dark patterns in popular social media mobile applications. The study analyzes how interface design is used to steer user behavior, capture attention, and exploit psychological vulnerabilities, often at the expense of user autonomy.
projects.challenges: Social media platforms are deeply embedded in everyday life, yet their interfaces often employ manipulative design strategies that users are unaware of. The challenge was to systematically identify and categorize dark patterns across multiple platforms, while translating academic research into insights relevant for design practice.
projects.solution: I conducted a structured interface audit of nine widely used social media mobile applications. Interactions were documented through screen recordings and analyzed using thematic analysis, guided by an established dark pattern ontology. The findings were synthesized into higher-level design strategies illustrating how user autonomy is undermined.
projects.outcome: The study identified 34 unique dark patterns, 13 of which were newly defined. The results highlight recurring design strategies such as obstruction, forced action, and social engineering. The project demonstrates how persuasive design techniques can shift from supporting user goals to exploiting attention, behavior, and psychological vulnerability.
projects.reflection: This research deepened my understanding of how design decisions compound over time. It reinforced my commitment to ethical design practices and the importance of questioning design patterns that might serve business goals at the expense of user autonomy.

images.title: Dark Pattern Taxonomy
images.description: The research framework categorizes manipulative design patterns into distinct strategies such as obstruction, forced action, social engineering, and interface interference. This systematic approach enabled consistent identification across platforms.
images.alt: Diagram showing the taxonomy and classification framework for dark patterns

images.title: Real-World Dark Patterns
images.description: Screen recordings from nine major social media platforms revealed 34 distinct dark patterns, including 13 newly identified techniques. Examples ranged from hidden unsubscribe options to manipulative notification patterns and forced engagement loops.
images.alt: Collection of documented dark pattern examples from social media applications

projects.title: Fullstack E-commerce Website for naima
projects.description: A modern, accessible fullstack web application for Naima, a Swedish superfood fika brand. The site combines brand storytelling with e-commerce functionality, featuring an interactive retailer map, wholesale partner dashboard, and comprehensive product showcase.
projects.fullDescription: Detailed multi-paragraph description for the project detail page. A modern, accessible fullstack web application for Naima, a Swedish superfood fika brand. The site combines brand storytelling with e-commerce functionality, featuring an interactive retailer map, wholesale partner dashboard, and comprehensive product showcase.
projects.challenges: The main challenge was creating a dual-purpose platform that served both B2C customers looking for products and B2B wholesale partners needing account management. Additionally, integrating a dynamic retailer map while maintaining fast load times required careful optimization.
projects.solution: I implemented a modular component architecture using React and Zustand for state management, allowing seamless switching between customer and wholesale views. For the retailer map, I used lazy loading and optimized API calls. The backend was built with Node.js and MongoDB to handle user authentication, product management, and wholesale orders efficiently.
projects.outcome: The website successfully launched with positive feedback from both customers and wholesale partners. Load times stayed under 2 seconds, the retailer map increased store visits by 30%, and the wholesale portal streamlined B2B operations significantly.

projects.title: Portfolio
projects.alt: Portfolio website showcasing projects and design work
projects.description: You're looking at it. This is a showcase of user-centered design in action.
projects.fullDescription: The second version of my portfolio, designed and built from scratch with React, Vite and Styled Components. Beyond presenting my work, the site is a project in itself: a place to make, test and document frontend decisions about architecture, performance and accessibility.
projects.metaDescription: How I designed and built my portfolio with React and Vite: a data-driven content model, a performance sprint, and the trade-offs behind the loading screen.
projects.problem:
What I enjoy most about coding is thinking in components: building something once and letting it vary. My first portfolio wasn't built that way, and version 2.0 was my chance to change that.

I wanted a portfolio that was easy to develop and easy to update. A portfolio is never finished: projects are added, descriptions are rewritten, and some projects grow into full case studies. If every change meant editing layout code, the site would quickly fall behind my work.

The projects themselves made that harder. A frontend app needs a live site and a GitHub link, a UX case study needs a Figma prototype, and a research project needs a downloadable thesis. The challenge was to handle all of them with the same set of components, without building one-off pages.

At the same time, the site had to feel personal and still load fast, and performance had to be something I measured rather than assumed.
projects.insight:
Performance is a design decision, not only a technical one.

The site opens with a full-screen loading screen. It sets the tone, but it delays first paint by roughly 2.75 seconds and lowers the Lighthouse performance score to around 40–55. Every other optimization on the site is in place, so the loading screen is the one deliberate cost.

So I made the wait do real work. While the animation plays, the code for the home page downloads in the background. The counter runs quickly to 90%, then slows to a crawl until that code has arrived, and only reaches 100% when the page is ready to render. The number on screen reflects actual progress, not a timer. Before any JavaScript has loaded, a static splash screen in the HTML covers the gap, so there is never a blank page.

Rather than removing it, I limited where it costs the most: it now runs once per session, and page transitions no longer fade in, so moving around the site after the first visit feels instant.
projects.approach:
A performance sprint. Routes are code-split and lazy loaded, and vendor libraries are split into separate chunks. An image script generates WebP versions in three sizes, served through srcset with a shimmer placeholder. Fonts load asynchronously, and Framer Motion was removed from the hero to reduce the JavaScript that blocks the largest paint.

Pages that load before you click. Splitting the code means each page is downloaded separately, which could make navigation feel slower. To avoid that, the page you land on loads first, and the other main pages load in the background as soon as the browser is idle. Hovering over or focusing a link in the navigation starts the download immediately, so even on a slow connection the next page is usually ready by the time it is clicked. Hovering over Projects also fetches the images for the first project cards, using the same srcset and sizes as the cards themselves, so the browser downloads exactly the variant it will show.
projects.contentAsData:
No project is written into a component. All projects live in a single JSON file, and each entry decides how its card looks: its size in the grid, which buttons it shows (GitHub, live site, prototype, PDF), and whether it links to a case study. A field that is left out simply means the button is not there.

Case study pages, including this one, are generated from the same entries through a custom hook, and a small config file works as a feature flag for pages that are still in progress. Adding a project means writing data, not code.

Try it below. The controls change this portfolio's own entry from the data, and the card underneath is the same ProjectCard component the Projects page uses.
projects.designSystem:
Colors, spacing, typography and breakpoints are defined once as CSS custom properties and shared styled-components mixins. Every component reads from the same tokens, so a change in one place carries through the whole site.

Layouts are mobile-first with min-width breakpoints, and spacing tokens grow with the screen: section padding goes from 1rem on a phone to 16rem on a wide desktop. Components such as the Button keep the interface consistent: one component with primary, secondary and tertiary variants that renders as a router link, an external link or a native button depending on its props, and marks links that open a new tab or download a file.

The overview below is not a screenshot. It is rendered from the site's live tokens, so the values you see are the ones the site is using right now.
projects.accessibility:
Accessibility is built into the components rather than added page by page. The same Button component renders internal routes, external links, icon-only links and file downloads, and each case gets what it needs to be understood without seeing it.

Links that open a new tab show an icon and announce "(opens in new tab)" through visually hidden text. Icon-only buttons have no visible text, so their label moves to aria-label. PDF links are marked as downloads. One global rule gives every interactive element the same visible focus outline, shown only for keyboard focus. Every animation respects the reduced motion setting: a single MotionConfig turns movement off in all Framer Motion animations while fades remain, a global CSS rule does the same for CSS animations and smooth scrolling, and the loading screen and experience timeline have their own reduced versions on top.

The overview below renders the real buttons and reads their accessible names from the page, the same text a screen reader would announce.

bundleSizes._note: Gzipped JavaScript from production builds of each version, measured October 2026

projects.outcome:
The performance sprint cut the JavaScript loaded on first visit by 21%, from 141 kB to 112 kB gzipped. Before it, React and all of my own code shipped as a single 72 kB chunk; after it, my own startup code was down to 13 kB.

Measuring again for this case study revealed a regression. I had later added a barrel file that re-exports every component from one place. Because the app's entry point imported through it, the bundler treated every component as startup code, including pages and demos that are only needed later. My own startup code had grown to 36 kB. Importing components file by file in the entry point brought it back down to 12 kB.

Today the first visit loads 121 kB, 14% less than before the sprint, even though the loading screen needs Framer Motion from the first frame. The total JavaScript across the site is 159 kB, 24% less than where it started, interactive demos on this page included.

Lighthouse scores of 95+ for accessibility and 100 for best practices and SEO, with performance traded off knowingly for the loading screen.

Adding a new project takes one JSON entry and one image. A full case study takes a few more fields, with no new components.
projects.reflection:
Building the site over a year, in phases rather than all at once, put the component approach to the test. My own work kept changing what the site needed: first a place for frontend projects, then case studies, then an About page. Each addition built on what was already there instead of replacing it.

Writing this case study became a review of its own. Every claim had to hold up against the code, and checking them uncovered an image preload that never ran, animations that ignored the reduced motion setting, and a barrel file that had tripled my startup code. All three are fixed, and the text now describes exactly what the site does.

The most useful lesson was to measure before optimizing, and to treat every trade-off as a choice I can explain, including the ones that lower a score.

In the end, this page sums up the project better than any paragraph. It is generated from a single entry in projects.json, and the demos above are the same components the rest of the site is built from. A case study about thinking in components, made of them.
